A person with mental problems is more likely to shoot up a school than a sane person. A person with mental problems is also more likely to be on some kind of antidepressant or antipsychotic. My take on that is that it is the mental problem that is the root cause.

That said, during the first month or so after a newly introduced antidepressant there is an increased risk for suicide or violent behaviour. The medication does not in itself introduce those thoughts and tendencies in the patient, they are there already. They simply make the patient better (not as often as we would like, but still) and more able to act on his thoughts, whatever they are. If a patient has a severe depression, those thoughts are usually a bit on the dark side. So before more normal thought patterns are established, shit can indeed go south. That is why a patient with a new psychiatric medication should have frequent follow-ups, something that isn't done nearly enough.

I love hearing people talk about the GameCube. It's one of those consoles that I've heard little but praise about since the Wii's launch, but whenever I look back to 2006 and earlier, it becomes hard to find GameCube fans. But I digress.

Nintendo began working on the GameCube in collaboration with the hardware company ArtX pretty quickly after the N64 was released. Groundwork was being laid in 1998, and Project Dolphin was announced in May 1999, over two years before the GameCube was released. It was finally given the name "GameCube" in August 2000, and unveiled their launch lineup at E3 2001. It was abbreviated NGC or GCN by Nintendo on a regional basis, apparently because they wanted "Nintendo" to be implied. Some of the more notable hardware features were the optical discs capable of storing much more data than cartridges, the classic Wavebird controller, and a surprising amount of power. The use of mini-discs instead of DVDs was a compromise between accommodating for third party support, fighting piracy, and keeping costs low. It worked: the GameCube was a more powerful machine than the PS2, despite its lower price point, and the GameCube library had nearly twice as many games released for it as the N64 despite lower lifetime sales..

People remember the early GameCube lineup fondly today, but in retrospect, there were only three games for the Japanese launch: Luigi's Mansion, Wave Race: Blue Storm, and Super Monkey Ball. The North American release also included Pikmin and Rogue Squadron 2, but Super Smash Bros Melee, arguably the GameCube's definitive game, was not released until November in Japan and December in America. Note the lack of a Super Mario game, something unheard of for Nintendo hardware at launch back then. Even the Game Boy Advance got an updated version of Doki Doki Panic.

Nintendo's early GameCube library can be connected to their transitioning from the Game Boy Color and N64 to the GBA and GameCube in a fairly short period. The N64 had a notable drought prior to the GameCube's launch, with Nintendo's biggest games being Dr Mario 64 and the first Japan-only version of Animal Crossing. Other Nintendo games released in the West during 2001, like Paper Mario and Pokemon Stadium 2, simpoly took a while to get here from Japan. Many early GameCube games were connected to projects that began on the N64. Animal Crossing, Kirby Air Ride, Eternal Darkness, Star Fox Adventures, and Doshin the Giant all began on the N64 before being released or otherwise better known on the GameCube.

This is not to say the GameCube relied heavily on N64 ports early on. In addition to the fairly strong launch window, 2002 brought three major releases: Super Mario Sunshine, The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker, and Metroid Prime. Sunshine would be one of the three best-selling games on the platform, along with Melee and Mario Kart. Wind Waker had a mixed initial response from fans, but has since become a favorite among many. Metroid Prime turned the dormant IP into a major series for Nintendo, winning critical acclaim and the best sales of any Metroid game ever released.

2003 was a relative lull for the GameCube, much like 2008 was for the Wii. Though Nintendo released Mario Kart: Double Dash, it seems to have overshadowed other racing games such as Kirby Air Ride and F-Zero: GX. This might have been what doomed that platform, because after 2003, GameCube sales fell across the world, even with price cuts. There were still great games released, especially in 2004 and early 2005. Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door, Metroid Prime 2, Pikmin 2, Pokemon Colosseum, and Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance were all well received by fans and critics. And with this decline, third party support also waned. Though Nintendo's level of support didn't falter until 2006, the GameCube had 109 new releases in 2005, compared to the 198 new releases in 2003.

One last question about the GameCube was whether it was successful at attracting third party support. The answer is complicated. On one hand, the GameCube had more games released than the N64, 662 rather than 388. Despite this, the GameCube only sold about 60% as well as the N64. Furthermore, third party support was sometimes lacking in the oddest ways. For example, Grand Theft Auto 3, one of the best-selling games of the era, was not brought to the GameCube even though the platform was more technically capable than the PS2 and the mini-discs, though smaller than a DVD, were entirely capable of containing games as large as GTA3's 1.2 GB. This is even more confusing considering how the GameCube's biggest market was North America, which was also the chief location of series fans. In other words, even when the hardware was available, third parties were not willing to work on Nintendo hardware. We also have the infamous "Capcom Five," a group of exclusives promised by Capcom for the GameCube. Of these, only one, the obscure PN03 ended up as a GameCube exclusive, while three (including Resident Evil 4) were ported to the PS2 and the last was cancelled. Oddly enough, the best-selling third party games were often from Sega, usually featuring Mario's longtime rival Sonic the Hedgehog.

So what effects did the GameCube have on Nintendo in the future? Mostly as an example of what not to do. The GameCube might have been what ultimately convinced Nintendo to drop out of the typical console arms race, instead opting for the Wii. The Wii sold better both in 2008 and 2009 than the GameCube sold in its entire lifetime, so that seems to have paid off. Future Nintendo hardware also put a greater emphasis on online capabilities, though often still well behind competitors. Even the original DS was far better online than the GameCube was. That said, the GameCube still showed up in interesting ways later on. The Wii was not just called "Two GameCubes taped together"because of its weakness, but also because it was essentially a boosted version of the existing GameCube hardware. Experiments with 3D effects on the GameCube ultimately made the 3DS possible.

And of course, the GameCube was a breeding ground creative new series and re-imaginings of older series. Pikmin, Animal Crossing, Metroid Prime, Wind Waker, Four Swords Adventures, and other Nintendo games broke expectations, and created new ones in the process. And in the upcoming Wii/DS generation, the ground set on the GameCube would be invaluable. Animal Crossing flourished in Wild World, but didn't start on the DS. EAD Tokyo, the makers of Super Mario Galaxy, started with a Donkey Kong platformer based on a drum peripheral on the GameCube. Minigame collections on the Wii were influenced by the likes of Mario Party and WarioWare. So even if viewed as Nintendo's last "normal" console, the GameCube laid the roots for a great future.
